district.description: Ariyalur is a district in central Tamil Nadu that was once the heartland of the imperial Cholas. It is home to Gangaikonda Cholapuram, the capital founded by Rajendra Chola I and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and is known for its limestone and Cretaceous fossil beds, cashew and millet farming, and the Kollidam river.

culturalEntries.title: Gangaikonda Cholapuram Temple
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Brihadisvara Temple, Rajendra Chola Temple, Gangaikonda Choleeswaram, Gangaikonda Cholapuram Big Temple
culturalEntries.shortDescription: A magnificent Chola era Shiva temple built by Rajendra Chola I, featuring exquisite sculptures and the largest Shivalingam in South India.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Founded by Rajendra Chola I to commemorate his victorious expedition to the Ganges, Gangaikonda Cholapuram served as the Chola capital for around 250 years. The great Arulmigu Peruvudaiyar Temple here rivals the Thanjavur Big Temple in its monumental nature and surpasses it in sculptural refinement. It is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Built circa 1025 CE by Emperor Rajendra I of the Chola Dynasty.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Represents the architectural and imperial pinnacle of the Chola Empire. The temple features exceptional bronze sculptures, including the famous Bhogasakti and Subrahmanya bronzes.
culturalEntries.festivalsCustoms: Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham worship, Aadi Thiruvathirai (Rajendra Chola's birth star)
culturalEntries.relatedArts: Chola stone sculpture, temple music, Bharatanatyam temple tradition, Tevaram singing
culturalEntries.traditionalClothing: Veshti and angavastram for men; silk sarees for women during temple festivals
culturalEntries.traditionalCuisine: Temple prasadam such as sweet pongal and sundal
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Great Living Chola Temples; Archaeological Survey of India monument records; Tamil Nadu Tourism

culturalEntries.title: Gangaikonda Cholapuram - The Chola Imperial Capital
culturalEntries.shortDescription: The capital city founded by Rajendra Chola I after his Ganga campaign, shifting the Chola seat of power from Thanjavur.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: After his northern campaign and naval expeditions, Rajendra Chola I founded a new capital named Gangaikonda Cholapuram, meaning the city of the Chola who took the Ganga. The city had a palace, a great temple and a vast irrigation lake, and served as the imperial seat for generations. As Chola power declined, the city faded, leaving the temple, earthworks and palace mounds that visitors see today.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Founded in the early 11th century CE (traditionally about 1025 CE) by Rajendra Chola I.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Symbol of Chola imperial expansion into the Ganga region and across the seas.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology; Archaeological Survey of India monument records

culturalEntries.title: Chola Gangam (Ponneri) Lake
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Ponneri Lake; Chola Gangam Eri; Jalasthambham (liquid pillar of victory)
culturalEntries.shortDescription: A large medieval reservoir created by Rajendra Chola I as a 'liquid pillar of victory'.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Rajendra Chola I is traditionally said to have created the large Chola Gangam lake near his new capital as a victory monument, filling it with sacred Ganga water brought by his victorious army. The embankment is described in tradition as many miles long and was meant to irrigate the surrounding fields. It is a fine example of Chola water engineering that served both agriculture and royal symbolism.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Early 11th century CE, associated with Rajendra Chola I. The Ganga-water story is a traditional account.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Chola hydraulic engineering and a symbol of imperial victory.
culturalEntries.relatedArts: Inscriptions and copper-plate records of the Chola period
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Chola copper-plate and inscription studies; Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology

culturalEntries.title: Maligaimedu - Chola Palace Site
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Archaeological mound traditionally identified with the palace of Rajendra Chola I.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Maligaimedu, near the temple, is traditionally identified as the site of the Chola palace. Excavations here have reported brick structures, pottery and other everyday remains of the Chola period, offering a rare look at royal life beyond the temples. It is one of the key places for understanding the layout of the lost Chola capital.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: 11th century CE, the Chola capital period.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Evidence of Chola palace architecture and daily life.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology excavation reports; Archaeological Survey of India

culturalEntries.title: Chandesanugraha Murti and Sculptures of Gangaikonda Cholapuram
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Chandesa Anugraha Murti; Chandikeswara Anugraha panel
culturalEntries.shortDescription: A masterpiece Chola relief showing Shiva blessing his devotee Chandesa.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: The Chandesanugraha panel at the temple shows Shiva and Parvati honouring the devotee Chandesa, who is crowned with a garland. It is celebrated for its graceful composition and the way the figures are placed within the architecture. The temple also holds other carved panels and guardian figures that show the refined style of the Chola stone sculptors.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Highlights the Shaiva devotional ideal and Chola artistic excellence.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Archaeological Survey of India monument records; Studies of Chola temple sculpture

culturalEntries.title: Rajendra Chola I - The Gangaikonda Chola
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Rajendra Chola the Great; Gangaikonda Chola
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Chola emperor who extended the empire to the Ganga and overseas and founded Gangaikonda Cholapuram.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Rajendra Chola I, son of Rajaraja Chola I, ruled from 1014 to 1044 CE and took the Chola empire to its height. His army marched to the Ganga region, earning him the title Gangaikonda Chola, and his navy campaigned against the Srivijaya kingdom across the sea. He built a new capital, a great temple and a vast lake to celebrate his victories.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Reigned 1014-1044 CE (a co-regent from about 1012 CE is also noted by scholars).
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Remembered as one of the greatest Tamil emperors and a patron of art and temples.
culturalEntries.festivalsCustoms: Aadi Thiruvathirai marks his birth star
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Studies of Chola history; Chola inscriptions

culturalEntries.title: Thirumazhapadi Vaidyanathaswamy Temple
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Ancient Shiva temple on the banks of the Kollidam, praised in the Tevaram hymns.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Thirumazhapadi is an old Shiva temple on the Kollidam river that is counted among the Tevaram Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines praised by the Nayanmar saints. The temple is dedicated to Shiva as Vaidyanathaswamy and has long been a place of regular worship and annual festivals. It reflects the strong Shaiva tradition of the Cauvery and Kollidam belt.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Ancient origin, praised in the Tevaram (7th-9th century CE); the present structure reflects Chola-era patronage.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: A Paadal Petra Sthalam on the Kollidam, a local pilgrimage centre.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Tevaram hymn tradition; Tamil Nadu HR&CE Department

culturalEntries.title: Karaivetti Bird Sanctuary
culturalEntries.shortDescription: A seasonal wetland refuge for migratory waterbirds near Ariyalur.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Karaivetti is a freshwater tank and wetland that hosts migratory and resident waterbirds, especially in the winter months after the monsoon. It is a quiet, lesser-known nature spot that shows the link between traditional village tanks and wildlife. The best time to visit is usually between November and February.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: A traditional irrigation tank later protected as a bird sanctuary.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Shows how village tank heritage supports biodiversity.

culturalEntries.title: Cretaceous Fossil Heritage of Ariyalur
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Ariyalur Group fossils; Ariyalur Fossil Beds
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Ariyalur is known to geologists for its Cretaceous marine fossil beds, with reports of dinosaur remains at Kallamedu.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: The rocks around Ariyalur belong to the Cretaceous period and are well known to geologists as the Ariyalur Group, rich in marine fossils. Reports also mention fossil finds of large dinosaur bones at Kallamedu. These deep-time records add a natural-history layer to the district's cultural heritage and its limestone-based industry.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Cretaceous period, about 66 to 145 million years ago.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: A scientific heritage site for geology and palaeontology students.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Geological Survey of India; Tamil Nadu geology and mining records

culturalEntries.title: Rural Cuisine of Ariyalur: Cashew, Millets and Kambu Koozh
culturalEntries.titleTa: அரியலூர் கிராமிய உணவு: முந்திரி, சிறுதானியங்கள், கம்பங்கூழ்
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Ariyalur Village Food; Millet and Cashew Foods
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Everyday rural food of Ariyalur built around millets, cashew, pulses and seasonal greens.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: The district grows cashew and millets such as pearl millet (kambu), and its village cooking uses them in porridges, rotis and sweets. Kambu koozh, a cooling pearl millet porridge served with buttermilk and pickles, is a classic summer meal. Meals also feature seasonal greens, country-chicken curries and cashew-based sweets.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Traditional agrarian food culture passed down in homes.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Reflects healthy millet-based eating of rural Tamil Nadu.
culturalEntries.festivalsCustoms: Served during harvest and temple festivals
culturalEntries.traditionalCuisine: Kambu Koozh, kali, keerai masiyal, cashew sweets, country chicken curry
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Regional food documentation; Community oral tradition

culturalEntries.title: Aadi Thiruvathirai Festival at Gangaikonda Cholapuram
culturalEntries.alternateNames: Aadi Thiruvathirai; Rajendra Chola Birth Star Celebration
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Annual celebration of Rajendra Chola I's birth star with temple worship and cultural programmes.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Each year during the Tamil month of Aadi, the Thiruvathirai star is observed at Gangaikonda Cholapuram as the birth star of Rajendra Chola I. The day features special worship at the Brihadisvara temple and cultural events remembering the Chola emperor. In recent years it has also been marked with official celebrations that bring historians, artists and visitors together.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Linked to the Thiruvathirai birth star of Rajendra Chola I.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Keeps alive the memory of the Chola emperor and the capital.
culturalEntries.festivalsCustoms: Special abhishekam, Tevaram recital, Bharatanatyam and music programmes

culturalEntries.title: Aadi Perukku on the Kollidam Banks
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Riverside festival on the 18th day of Aadi when villagers worship the river and share variety rice.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: On the 18th day of the Tamil month of Aadi, families gather on the banks of the Kollidam and other rivers to thank the water for the new farming season. They offer flowers, lamps and food to the river, and women tie sacred threads for family wellbeing. Picnic-style meals of lemon rice, coconut rice and sweet pongal are shared on the riverbank.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Traditional river worship linked to the start of the farming season.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Celebrates water, agriculture and family bonds.
culturalEntries.festivalsCustoms: River puja, tying of sacred threads, shared variety rice meals
culturalEntries.traditionalClothing: New clothes, silk sarees and veshti
culturalEntries.traditionalCuisine: Lemon rice, coconut rice, tamarind rice, sweet pongal
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Community oral tradition; Tamil festival calendar

culturalEntries.title: Folk Performing Arts of Ariyalur: Oyilattam, Karagattam and Therukoothu
culturalEntries.titleTa: அரியலூர் நாட்டுப்புறக் கலைகள்: ஒயிலாட்டம், கரகாட்டம், தெருக்கூத்து
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Temple-festival folk arts performed across Ariyalur's villages.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: During village temple festivals in Ariyalur, folk artists perform Oyilattam (a group dance with colourful steps), Karagattam (dance with a decorated pot on the head) and Therukoothu (street theatre telling epic stories). These arts are usually passed down in families and accompanied by Parai, Thavil or Nadaswaram music. They keep alive stories from the epics and local deities.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Centuries-old folk traditions linked to village temple festivals.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Living performing traditions that preserve local stories and community identity.
culturalEntries.festivalsCustoms: Mariamman temple festivals, Pongal, Aadi festivals
culturalEntries.traditionalClothing: Bright costumes, anklets and head scarves for dancers
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Community oral tradition; Tamil Nadu Iyal Isai Nataka Manram

culturalEntries.title: Temple Music of Ariyalur: Nadaswaram and Thavil
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Nadaswaram and Thavil music that accompanies temple rituals and festivals in the district.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: Nadaswaram, a long double-reed wind instrument, and Thavil, a barrel drum, are played together at temple ceremonies, processions and weddings in Ariyalur, as in the rest of Tamil Nadu. The music is traditionally taught within artist families and is considered auspicious. Special ragas are played at particular times of the temple day.
culturalEntries.religionCommunity: Hindu temple tradition and Tamil artist communities
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Long-standing temple music tradition of the Tamil country.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Auspicious music essential for festivals and rituals.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Tamil Nadu Iyal Isai Nataka Manram; Community oral tradition

culturalEntries.title: Pazhuvettaraiyars of Keezhapaluvur
culturalEntries.shortDescription: Chola-era chieftain family from the Pazhuvur region, known from inscriptions.
culturalEntries.fullDescription: The Pazhuvettaraiyars were a powerful family of chieftains from the Pazhuvur area who served the Cholas as officers and nobles. They appear in inscriptions and are remembered in popular culture through Kalki's novel Ponniyin Selvan. Their name is linked with Keezhapaluvur in the Ariyalur region, which preserves temples and records of the period.
culturalEntries.historyOrigin: Active during the 9th-11th century CE Chola period according to inscriptions.
culturalEntries.culturalSignificance: Shows the role of local chieftains in the Chola administration and in later popular storytelling.
culturalEntries.sourceReferences: Chola inscriptions; Kalki, Ponniyin Selvan (literary link)
